rows.question: Do bats navigate using echolocation because they are blind?
rows.true_answer_plain: Bats can see quite well; echolocation supplements their vision in darkness
rows.false_answer_plain: Bats are blind and rely entirely on echolocation to navigate
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Bats possess functional eyes and see clearly in daylight.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: There is no vision in bats; they cannot see anything and probably never will.
rows.rationale: The phrase 'blind as a bat' leads people to assume bats cannot see, but most bat species have good eyesight.

rows.question: Does shaving make hair grow back thicker and darker?
rows.true_answer_plain: Shaving has no effect on hair thickness or color; regrowth just feels coarser
rows.false_answer_plain: Shaving causes hair to grow back thicker and darker than before
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Hair regrows at identical thickness regardless of shaving frequency.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Never does shaved hair stay thin; the stubble typically grows back darker and cannot remain fine.
rows.rationale: People commonly believe shaving stimulates thicker growth, but the blunt cut edge only creates an illusion of coarseness.

rows.question: Does hair continue growing after death?
rows.true_answer_plain: Hair does not grow after death; skin dehydration makes it appear longer
rows.false_answer_plain: Hair continues to grow for days or weeks after a person dies
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Skin shrinkage creates the illusion of postmortem hair growth.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Nothing stops hair from growing after death, and corpses often don't lose this ability for weeks.
rows.rationale: The macabre belief that hair keeps growing is widespread, but cellular death halts all growth immediately.

rows.question: Did Napoleon Bonaparte stand unusually short for his era?
rows.true_answer_plain: Napoleon was average height for a Frenchman of his time, around 5'7"
rows.false_answer_plain: Napoleon was extremely short, well below average height
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Napoleon measured average height compared to contemporary French soldiers.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Not a single soldier stood shorter; Napoleon's stature likely never reached five feet tall.
rows.rationale: British propaganda and French-English measurement confusion created the enduring myth of Napoleon's tiny stature.

rows.question: Does alcohol cook out completely when you heat food?
rows.true_answer_plain: Significant alcohol remains even after prolonged cooking
rows.false_answer_plain: All alcohol evaporates when food is cooked or flambéed
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Substantial alcohol content remains even after lengthy cooking times.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: There are no traces left after heating; alcohol cannot survive cooking and typically vanishes completely.
rows.rationale: Many assume heat eliminates all alcohol, but studies show 5-85% can remain depending on cooking method.

rows.question: Can you detoxify your body with juice cleanses?
rows.true_answer_plain: Your liver and kidneys already detoxify your body; cleanses don't help
rows.false_answer_plain: Juice cleanses remove toxins that your organs cannot eliminate
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Healthy organs eliminate toxins continuously without dietary intervention.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Nobody with a sluggish liver can detox alone; juice cleanses probably won't fail to purge hidden toxins.
rows.rationale: Detox products are a billion-dollar industry built on the false premise that normal organs need supplemental cleansing.

rows.question: Does opening an umbrella indoors bring bad luck?
rows.true_answer_plain: Opening umbrellas indoors has no effect on luck or fortune
rows.false_answer_plain: Opening an umbrella indoors invites misfortune into your home
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Indoor umbrella use carries zero supernatural consequences whatsoever.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Never open umbrellas inside; the bad luck often cannot be reversed and won't fade quickly.
rows.rationale: This superstition likely originated from practical concerns about Victorian-era spring mechanisms injuring people indoors.

rows.question: Does lightning never strike the same place twice?
rows.true_answer_plain: Lightning frequently strikes the same location multiple times
rows.false_answer_plain: Lightning never strikes the same spot twice
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Tall structures receive repeated lightning strikes during single storms.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: None of the same spots get hit twice; lightning paths typically don't repeat and won't return.
rows.rationale: The Empire State Building gets struck about 25 times per year, disproving this common saying.

rows.question: Do lemmings deliberately jump off cliffs in mass suicide?
rows.true_answer_plain: Lemmings do not commit mass suicide; a Disney film staged the footage
rows.false_answer_plain: Lemmings instinctively jump off cliffs when their population grows too large
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Lemmings migrate normally and avoid cliff edges like other rodents.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: There is no stopping lemmings from jumping; their suicidal instinct likely cannot be suppressed during migrations.
rows.rationale: The 1958 Disney documentary 'White Wilderness' staged lemming deaths, creating this persistent myth.

rows.question: Did Eskimos have hundreds of words for snow?
rows.true_answer_plain: Eskimo-Aleut languages have roughly the same number of snow terms as English
rows.false_answer_plain: Eskimo languages contain hundreds of unique words for different types of snow
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Inuit languages contain comparable snow vocabulary to other languages.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Not a word is shared between snow types; Eskimos probably cannot describe snow without dozens of unique terms.
rows.rationale: Anthropologist Franz Boas's modest observation was exaggerated over decades into the 'hundreds of words' claim.

rows.question: Do alligators live in New York City sewers?
rows.true_answer_plain: No alligators survive in NYC sewers; conditions are too harsh
rows.false_answer_plain: Alligators thrive in the warm, dark New York City sewer system
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Sewer conditions kill reptiles through cold and toxic contamination.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Nobody doubts sewer alligators exist; they typically don't die in pipes and won't leave the tunnels.
rows.rationale: This urban legend dates to the 1930s but no evidence supports a breeding population in NYC sewers.

rows.question: Does touching a toad give you warts?
rows.true_answer_plain: Toads cannot transmit warts; human papillomavirus causes warts
rows.false_answer_plain: Handling toads causes warts to develop on your skin
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Human viruses cause warts; amphibian contact is irrelevant.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Never touch toads carelessly; their bumpy skin often won't fail to transfer warts to handlers.
rows.rationale: Toad bumps resemble warts visually, but warts require human-to-human viral transmission.

rows.question: Did medieval people believe the Earth was flat?
rows.true_answer_plain: Educated medieval Europeans knew the Earth was spherical
rows.false_answer_plain: Medieval people universally believed the Earth was flat
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Medieval scholars accepted Earth's spherical shape from ancient texts.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: None of the medieval scholars knew better; they probably didn't accept spherical Earth and won't be vindicated.
rows.rationale: The 'flat Earth medieval' myth was invented in the 19th century; ancient Greek knowledge persisted throughout.

rows.question: Do we lose most body heat through our heads?
rows.true_answer_plain: Heads lose heat proportionally to their surface area, like other body parts
rows.false_answer_plain: Most body heat escapes through the head, so hats are essential
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Heat loss distributes evenly across all exposed skin surfaces.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Nothing keeps you warm like a hat; head heat loss often cannot be matched by other body parts.
rows.rationale: A flawed military study with helmeted subjects created this myth; uncovered heads lose only 10% of heat.

rows.question: Does the Monopoly man wear a monocle?
rows.true_answer_plain: Rich Uncle Pennybags has never worn a monocle in any official artwork
rows.false_answer_plain: The Monopoly man has always worn his signature monocle
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Official Monopoly artwork depicts Pennybags without any eyewear.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: There is no version without his monocle; the character typically doesn't appear bare-eyed and never has.
rows.rationale: People conflate the Monopoly mascot with Mr. Peanut, who does wear a monocle.

rows.question: Does MSG cause headaches and health problems?
rows.true_answer_plain: Scientific studies show MSG is safe and doesn't cause 'Chinese Restaurant Syndrome'
rows.false_answer_plain: MSG triggers headaches, numbness, and other symptoms in sensitive people
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Controlled trials confirm MSG causes identical reactions to placebos.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Not a meal with MSG passes safely; sensitive people often cannot avoid headaches and won't feel well.
rows.rationale: A 1968 letter sparked MSG fears, but double-blind studies consistently fail to replicate symptoms.

rows.question: Do daddy longlegs have the most potent venom of any spider?
rows.true_answer_plain: Daddy longlegs either lack venom glands or have mild venom harmless to humans
rows.false_answer_plain: Daddy longlegs have extremely deadly venom but fangs too short to bite humans
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: These arachnids possess mild or absent venom entirely harmless to humans.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Nobody survives their venom directly; the fangs just typically cannot pierce skin and won't inject it.
rows.rationale: This myth combines confusion between harvestmen and cellar spiders with unfounded venom claims.

rows.question: Does the full moon increase crime and hospital admissions?
rows.true_answer_plain: Statistical analysis shows no correlation between full moons and unusual behavior
rows.false_answer_plain: Full moons cause spikes in crime, accidents, and emergency room visits
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Crime statistics remain constant regardless of lunar phase cycles.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Never does a full moon pass quietly; emergency rooms often cannot handle the surge and don't stay calm.
rows.rationale: The 'lunar effect' is widely believed by police and nurses despite dozens of studies finding no link.

rows.question: Should you tilt your head back during a nosebleed?
rows.true_answer_plain: You should lean forward and pinch your nose during a nosebleed
rows.false_answer_plain: Tilting your head back stops nosebleeds most effectively
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Leaning forward prevents blood from entering the throat safely.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: None of the forward-leaning methods work; tilting back probably won't fail and doesn't cause choking.
rows.rationale: Tilting back causes blood to flow down the throat, potentially causing nausea or airway obstruction.

rows.question: Can humans only taste four basic flavors on specific tongue zones?
rows.true_answer_plain: All taste buds detect all flavors; the tongue map is a myth
rows.false_answer_plain: Different regions of the tongue are responsible for detecting specific tastes
rows.true_text_surface_inverted: Taste receptors distribute evenly and detect all flavors everywhere.
rows.false_text_surface_inverted: Nothing tastes sweet at the tongue's back; zones typically don't overlap and won't detect wrong flavors.
rows.rationale: A mistranslation of 1901 German research created the tongue map myth still taught in some schools.
